text: Declare, fill, read back: size, memory and indexing.
One variable holds only its last value. An **array** keeps every value, and because the index is a variable, a loop can reach any box in any order.
`int a[N]` has boxes `a[0]` to `a[N-1]`. There is no `a[N]`.
Where you declare an array decides what is in it at the start.
A local array is not zeroed: write `= {}` or call `fill`. With many test cases, reset only the first n boxes with `fill(a, a + n, 0)`, not the whole array each time.
Contest code often uses `memset` from C instead. It is fast, but it fills **bytes**, not ints.
Declare big arrays **global**: they start at 0 and do not overflow the stack. Size with a margin: `int a[1005]` for n ≤ 1000.
Pick 0 based or 1 based indexing, and keep it for the whole program.

Reading past the end (`a[n]`, `a[-1]`) does not crash reliably. It reads a neighbour or garbage, and the bug shows up far away. A reverse loop that starts at `i = n` prints one value that was never filled.
Tables a[i][j], 3D arrays, and lookup tables.
Think of a **table**: the first index picks the row, the second the column. Read and print with two nested loops, rows outside and columns inside.
`int g[105][105]` is about 44 KB. A grid of characters is easiest as `string g[N]`: read one row with `cin >> g[i]`, and `g[i][j]` is still row i, column j.
A third index works the same way, with a third loop (P5729).
Fixed pictures go in a lookup table. Output is built **row by row** of the screen.
The outer loop is the screen row, the inner loop walks the items. This is P5730.
Records and counters, pairs and windows, grid walks, transforms and encodings.
Let the **index be the thing itself**: a position, or a value.
Record: `mark[p] = 1` says position p has some property. Setting it twice leaves it at 1, so overlaps are handled for free.
Counter: `cnt[v]++` says you saw value v once more. One step per value, no searching.
Negative values need a shift: value v lives at `v + 100`.
`x ^= 1` flips a box between 0 and 1.
Counting by value also sorts: walk the indexes in order and print each value cnt times.
Every element against every other: outer `i`, inner `j = i + 1`. That visits each pair **exactly once**, and never an element with itself.
n(n − 1) / 2 pairs is O(n²): fine up to n ≈ 5000.
Pairs plus a record array: mark every sum first, then ask once per value.
A value made by several pairs is still counted once, which is what "how many numbers" questions want (P2141).

title: A window of m consecutive values

text: Recomputing every window costs O(n·m). **Sliding** costs O(n): the next window is this one, plus the new right value, minus the old left one.
Each row is built from the row above it. Here: Pascal's triangle.
The zero padding in row 0 and column 0 makes every row start and end with 1, with no if (P5732).

title: Walking a grid with direction arrays

text: A direction becomes a number d. Moving is `x += dx[d], y += dy[d]`. Turning right is `d = (d + 1) % 4`.
Eight directions find all neighbours of a cell, as in minesweeper.
Check the bounds **before** reading `g[ni][nj]`. Or use 1 based storage with a padding border so every neighbour exists (P1789).
Write each transform as "where does cell (i, j) go?". Then 180° is 90° twice, and combinations are transforms applied one after another.
Never rotate **in place**: writing into `a` while still reading it destroys cells you need. Build the result in a second array, then copy it back (P1205).
In C, a character grid is `char g[N][N]`, and a whole array is copied with `memcpy`.
Store a 0 and 1 sequence as the **lengths of its runs**. By convention the first run counts 0s, so a sequence starting with 1 begins with a run of length 0 (P1319, P1320).
